The opposition is a collection of minority parties, which can agree on almost no issue, but may be able to come together to defeat the government on a vote - which essentially usually forces the need for an election.

In British parliamentary politics, the ruling government must command the confidence of the house, which means they have to be able to control enough votes in order to pass legislation. If they fail to do this, they have lost the confidence of the house in their ability to govern the country. Traditionally, an election is held when confidence is lost, so as to hear the voice of the people, and elect new members to the house, so that a new government may be formed based on the results of that election, (mandate of the people.)

This is a scenario in Parliamentary politics where minority parties suddenly enjoy very enhanced bargaining power, because the big parties need them. If you can get your party to win even just one seat in the Parliament, the day may come when you can get your own legislation passed as part of a bigger deal.

For example, the Canadian New Democratic Party (socialists) have never held a majority government in Canada, but they were successful in getting Medicare (universal health care) passed into law by holding the balance of power for a Liberal minority government at the time.
